[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call and then we can jump in. Is this time still good?
[00:00:06] Lena: Yep, good here. We got a few people on the call.
[00:00:09] Mark: Mark here. Thanks.
[00:00:11] Priya: Priya, SRE.
[00:00:13] Tom: Tom, ML eng.
[00:00:15] Maya: Great. Goal for today is to triage the KV cache eviction and paging patterns you saw during the long-context runs, walk through hypotheses, and land on concrete telemetry and a pilot. Carlos will lead the runtime specifics.
[00:00:30] Carlos: Hi all. Quick context: Sierra ran the prompt simulation with ~8k token histories and saw bad tail latencies when the KV layer spilled. The pattern was evictions that looked like prefix collisions and then a sudden spike in SSD paging. We want to map request / prefix metadata to eviction events and tune prefetch/batching so the runtime doesn't thrash.
[00:00:48] Lena: Right, we had a baseline fine for shorter contexts but once we push to 6–12k tokens, throughput collapsed and latency spiked to multiple seconds per token. The KV telemetry shows a lot of 'evict' events followed by 'page-in' from disk.
[00:01:02] Carlos: Understood. A couple quick clarifications: are you using Redwood Private on your VPC, or a dedicated pool in our hosted offering?
[00:01:10] Mark: We're on your Private deployment — VPC connected, we're running the runtime on our on-prem nodes with your control plane.
[00:01:17] Ruth: Thanks for clarifying. That matters because disk type and local I/O will change the paging behavior.
[00:01:22] Tom: Our staging nodes are 2x A40s with NVMe local disks; the pilot will likely go to 2x A100s.
[00:01:30] Carlos: Good. NVMe is fine but we need to check bandwidth and concurrency. There are several flow paths to consider: 1) prefix canonicalization mismatch leading to duplicate prefixes and ineffective reuse; 2) eviction thresholds tuned too low for your working set; 3) prefetch heuristics being out-of-sync with your request pattern; 4) KV compaction / tombstones causing misaccounted capacity.
[00:01:53] Dr. Lena: Can you explain prefix canonicalization mismatch?
[00:01:55] Carlos: Sure. Basically, the runtime normalizes prefix keys to decide which KV entries to reuse. If your prompts have small variations — whitespace, metadata, or small tokens — the keys can be treated as different even though the KV cache semantics should match. That creates hot shards of similar prefixes that don't actually hit each other's cached KV, so you get lots of 'near-miss' inserts that push out true hot entries.
[00:02:20] Maya: We're seeing logs where the same logical conversation has a slightly different embed or key because the pre-tokenized boundary changed; that aligns with what you're describing, Tom?
[00:02:27] Tom: Yeah, we've got metadata headers that change per request (request-id, timestamp). We thought the runtime strips those but maybe our pre-hook isn't applied.
[00:02:35] Priya: We do have an edge filter that appends the trace id into the prompt for observability, that might be the culprit.
[00:02:41] Carlos: That would do it. Action: strip ephemeral metadata before prefix generation or add a canonicalization step to hashes.
[00:02:48] [00:03:00] Maya: Another thing we saw is eviction correlated with high concurrent prefix creation — lots of new prefixes per second. When the KV store reaches the spill threshold (we default to ~70% of capacity), the eviction policy is LRU-ish but with some per-shard heuristics. If you have a burst of unique prefixes the working set outgrows the in-memory capacity and we spill to disk. Paging then incurs the latency spike.
[00:03:20] Mark: Is there a way to avoid the disk page-in? We saw disk I/O saturate and tokens took 700–1200ms sometimes.
[00:03:27] Carlos: Yes. Two levers: increase in-memory capacity (bigger nodes or tune memory allocation), or improve prefix reuse / reduce prefix cardinality. We also have prefetch strategies that can proactively warm the KV for expected prefixes based on session affinity.
[00:03:40] Lena: We prefer not to increase memory yet until we understand the root cause — raising capacity is more expensive.
[00:03:46] Carlos: Makes sense. So let's focus on canonicalization and prefetch. For prefetch, the heuristic uses n-gram continuation probability combined with recent hit rates to decide which prefix to fetch. If your workload has long linear sessions (like chat threads), we can tune the window to prefetch the next few likely prefixes. But if you have many short sessions mixed in, aggressive prefetch can just bloat the working set.
[00:04:06] Tom: Our pattern is a mix — most sessions are long, but there's also periodic batch jobs that spin up thousands of short sessions for evaluation.
[00:04:13] Carlos: That mixing is a classic thrash scenario. We can recommend two things: 1) isolate batch evaluation to separate KV shards (or separate instances) so they don't pollute the production working set; 2) configure a conservative prefetch for the mixed pool, or run batch through a dedicated Dedicated/DPO node.
[00:04:30] Priya: For Private we can carve off a dedicated pool for batch — operators are fine with that.
[00:04:33] [00:04:45] Maya: There's also quantization behavior to consider. When we run 4-bit quantized model variants, the KV entries are smaller but compute patterns change and the kernel selection could alter cache locality due to different block sizes for KV shards. We've seen slight changes in eviction timing when customers flip quantization profiles mid-rollout.
[00:04:59] Mark: We're mostly on int8/16 variants. Not using 4-bit yet.
[00:05:02] Carlos: OK, less likely to be quant-related then. But worth noting for future. Another thing: KV compaction cycles. If the background compactor runs at the same time as a heavy workload, it can transiently increase I/O and also temporarily reduce available in-memory entries while it compacts. The compactor schedule is tunable.
[00:05:19] Ruth: We can share how to check compaction logs in the runbook.
[00:05:22] Dr. Lena: Can you walk us through the telemetry we should capture to prove whether it's canonicalization vs true cardinality pressure?
[00:05:28] Carlos: Yes. Minimum telemetry: per-prefix hash distributions (showing near-duplicates), prefix creation rate per-second, eviction count per-shard with victim prefix fingerprints, page-in latency histogram, and a trace tying specific requests to the eviction events — basically a causal chain: request X generated prefix Y → prefix Y inserted → eviction of prefix Z → subsequent request misses and pages Z back in. We also want the runtime's per-request KV hit/miss indicator annotated in traces.
[00:05:54] Tom: We have some of that but not the victim fingerprints correlated to requests.
[00:05:58] Carlos: We'll provide the instrumentation patch — it's a debug flag: KV_DETAILED_TRACING=true — it will include victim prefix samples and compact the logs into a per-hour artifact. It is more verbose, so only enable on staging.
[00:06:12] Mark: How much overhead does that add?
[00:06:14] Carlos: On throughput it's negligible if you log asynchronously; on disk it will increase log volume maybe 2–4x.
[00:06:19] Priya: That's fine for staging. We'll run it during the 24h test and post the logs.
[00:06:23] [00:06:35] Maya: Another potential is prefix shadowing due to different tokenization. If upstream tokenizers or whitespace normalization differs between the client pre-processing and the runtime, you can create different canonical keys.
[00:06:45] Tom: We do tokenization in the client to do early scoring. The runtime gets the already-tokenized pieces. Might be a mismatch with the tokenizer version.
[00:06:52] Carlos: Yep — confirm tokenizer version and the exact bytes used to hash the prefix. We'll add that to the checklist.
[00:06:57] Lena: Any quick mitigation we can do while we investigate?
[00:07:00] Carlos: Yes: 1) strip ephemeral headers (trace ids) before prefix hashes; 2) apply a short dedup window where near-equal prefixes are coalesced for 5–10s; 3) separate long-session traffic from batch evaluation. We can provide default config snippets for the runtime.
[00:07:14] Mark: Coalescing sounds risky for correctness. How does it affect semantics?
[00:07:18] Carlos: It's conservative — we only coalesce when prefix similarity exceeds a threshold and the session id matches. It's opt-in and has telemetry. It's primarily to avoid high-cardinality noise.
[00:07:26] Priya: Ok we can try that in staging.
[00:07:29] [00:07:40] Tom: About paging back — is there an ability to pre-warm the KV after a traffic spike? For example, after a nightly job we can run a warm-up job to repopulate hot prefixes.
[00:07:49] Carlos: Absolutely. We have a 'prefetch batch' tool that accepts a list of prefixes and warms them into memory. It's a CLI you can run in staging before peak periods. We'll share the script. It also supports running with concurrency controls to avoid IO storms.
[00:07:59] Maya: We'll attach the script to the runbook.
[00:08:02] [00:08:14] Dr. Lena: What about eviction policy? Can we switch from LRU-ish to a frequency based (LFU) or a hybrid? We have some very hot prefixes that are scanned frequently and should be Sticky.
[00:08:25] Carlos: We support a hybrid policy — frequency-weighted LRU — that biases toward prefixes with high miss-corrected hit rates. It requires maintaining a small counter per-prefix which costs memory, but for small working sets it's very effective. We can recommend parameters based on your hit-rate histogram.
[00:08:39] Tom: How do we measure 'corrected hit-rate'?
[00:08:41] Carlos: It's essentially hit_rate / expected_rate where expected_rate is the modeled traffic for that prefix. If a prefix is requested way more than predicted, it gets boosted.
[00:08:50] [00:09:02] Maya: Quick note — we noticed an edge case where KV shard reassignment during autoscaling can cause transient double-insert or missed eviction accounting which looks like a leak and then a big purge. That's less common in Private because you control scaling, but if your autoscaler is aggressive, we should coordinate compaction and reassignment windows.
[00:09:18] Mark: We're not autoscaling in staging right now. Everything is manual.
[00:09:21] Carlos: Good. That rules out reassignment noise.
[00:09:24] [00:09:40] Maya: OK, let's show a quick example trace from our lab that mimics your symptoms so you see the event chain. Carlos, do you want to screen-share? (note: transcript logs references a shared link)
[00:09:45] Carlos: I'll narrate — link to trace: https://redwood.internal/traces/ff-20251215-kv-debug-sample (shared)
[00:09:51] Carlos: Here you see request 0x9a with prefix P1 generated, P1 inserted, then shortly later P2 inserted; the shard hits the capacity threshold and evicts P1 (victim). A later request needs P1 and we page it from disk — big latency. Also note the fingerprint similarity between P1 and P1' differing only by metadata.
[00:10:12] Tom: That looks identical to our logs.
[00:10:14] Priya: That link is helpful.
[00:10:17] [00:10:30] Maya: So the agreed reproducible steps: 1) enable KV_DETAILED_TRACING on staging, run your 24h long-context workload; 2) run a warm prefetch after the large nightly batch and compare tail-latency; 3) we will provide canonicalization patch and a suggested config to add to your runtime; 4) if results still show paging, we'll spin up the 2x A100 pilot with dedicated memory set to 1.2x working set to see if it's purely memory bound.
[00:10:52] Lena: That plan works. On the pilot — what's the estimated timeline?
[00:10:56] Maya: If you confirm node spec this week we can provision and get baseline tests in out pilot env within ~7 business days.
[00:11:04] Mark: We can confirm by Friday.
[00:11:06] [00:11:20] Carlos: A few more low-level notes to capture: - check KV config: shard_count, spill_threshold_mb, eviction_window_seconds - enable victim fingerprint logging - capture per-shard free memory and file descriptor counts during the run - set prefetch max concurrent fetches to 16 for NVMe nodes - schedule compaction off-peak or reduce compaction aggressiveness during the test
[00:11:39] Priya: Will the debug flag expose PII? We need to verify data retention concerns.
[00:11:44] Carlos: By default we hash prefixes and only include first/last n bytes of the original to avoid full text in logs. We can redact further; we'll share the redaction policy.
[00:11:52] Ruth: We'll also provide the security docs (SOC 2) referenced earlier and the data handling appendix for Private deployments.
[00:11:58] [00:12:10] Tom: One more question: when the KV spill occurs, is the disk layout per-shard or global file store? We're concerned about contention across shards causing head-of-line I/O queuing.
[00:12:20] Carlos: In Private we default to per-shard files on NVMe to reduce contention; however, if the node's IO scheduler is contending across many concurrent small file writes, you can still see head-of-line. Our prefetch tool tries to schedule more sequential reads to mitigate this. We'll provide tuning for IO scheduler and recommended fio tests.
[00:12:39] Mark: Useful.
[00:12:41] [00:12:55] Maya: We're going to drop a short checklist and a link to the runbook in the notes. Also attach the prefetch script and the compaction schedule snippets.
[00:13:04] Carlos: I'll also drop a small patch that adds a canonicalization step (strip trace ids, normalize whitespace) that you can apply to your client-side preprocessor. It's non-invasive.
[00:13:13] Lena: Great. If after canonicalization and prefetch we still see paging, we'll probably opt to reserve more memory in pilot.
[00:13:19] Maya: Sounds good. Any blockers from the customer's side?
[00:13:23] Priya: We need final approval for enabling debug logs but already ok for staging.
[00:13:26] Tom: No blockers.
[00:13:28] [00:13:40] Maya: OK, recap of next steps (also in the action items): enable debug, run 24h trace, share logs, Redwood to provide runbook + prefetch script + canonicalization patch, schedule pilot after node confirmation.
[00:13:54] Lena: Thanks, appreciate the help.
[00:13:57] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the CRM and Slack channel.
